clinicalPearls: NHLs are cancers of mature B, T, and NK cells; ~90% are of B-cell origin. They are distinguished from Hodgkin's lymphoma by the absence of the Reed-Sternberg cell and differ from HL in biology, natural history, and the more variable prognosis (Harrison 22e p.857).

Clinically, NHL is grouped by behavior: indolent/slow-growing (e.g., follicular lymphoma, the most common indolent NHL), aggressive (DLBCL, the most common subtype overall, ~one-third of cases), and highly aggressive/most rapidly growing (Burkitt's lymphoma, doubling time <24 h). Mantle cell lymphoma is intermediate-grade (Harrison 22e p.857, 862).

The duration and pace of symptoms help distinguish aggressive from indolent disease, as does the presence or absence of 'B' symptoms — fevers, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss (>10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.860-861).

Most common presentation of follicular lymphoma is new, painless lymphadenopathy at multiple sites; most patients lack elevated LDH or B symptoms. Asymptomatic indolent disease should be observed, as treating asymptomatic patients does not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.863-864).
Serum LDH and serum beta-2-microglobulin are important independent prognostic factors in NHL and should be measured at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.860).

Aggressive lymphomas (DLBCL, Burkitt's) are potentially curable with combination chemotherapy, whereas most indolent lymphomas are very responsive to therapy but not ultimately curable in the vast majority of cases except in localized early-stage disease (Harrison 22e p.862-863).
harrison.pathophysiology: NHLs arise from mature B, T, or NK lymphocytes, with ~90% being B-cell neoplasms; transformation typically requires several genetic events. Characteristic chromosomal translocations create fusion or deregulated oncogenes: t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma (>85% of cases, necessary but not sufficient for transformation); MYC rearrangement at 8q24 in >95% of Burkitt's lymphoma (most often t(8;14) fusing MYC to IgH); and t(11;18) (API2-MLT) in MALT lymphoma. Gene-expression profiling subdivides DLBCL into germinal-center B-cell (GCB)-like and activated-B-cell (ABC)-like subtypes with differing prognoses. Several NHLs are linked to chronic antigenic stimulation or infection-driven immune dysregulation, and immunodeficiency states strongly predispose to (often EBV-associated) lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.857-863).
additionalDifferentials: Reactive follicular hyperplasia (major differential for follicular lymphoma on biopsy)
Lymphoid leukemias (CLL/SLL, ALL), plasma cell disorders (multiple myeloma)
Other causes of lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or B-symptom-like constitutional illness
infectionMimics: Infectious mononucleosis / EBV infection and other viral lymphadenopathies
Multicentric Castleman's disease (HHV-8), which causes diffuse lymphadenopathy with fever, malaise, and weight loss mimicking lymphoma B symptoms
nonInfectiousMimics: Autoimmune disease with lymphadenopathy (e.g., Sjögren's syndrome, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis)
Sarcoidosis and other causes of constitutional symptoms with adenopathy
additionalInvestigations: Adequate tissue biopsy reviewed by an expert hematopathologist (follicular lymphoma and Burkitt's lymphoma can be diagnosed on morphology; immunophenotyping required) (Harrison 22e p.860, 863)
Complete blood count, routine chemistries, liver function tests, uric acid, calcium
Serum protein electrophoresis (to detect monoclonal paraproteins)
Serum LDH and serum beta-2-microglobulin (prognostic) (Harrison 22e p.860)
CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (essential for staging, especially indolent lymphomas) (Harrison 22e p.861)
FDG-PET (preferred for aggressive lymphomas such as DLBCL and Burkitt's, and to assess suspected transformation of indolent disease) (Harrison 22e p.861)
Lumbar puncture in lymphoblastic, Burkitt's, and DLBCL with positive marrow biopsy or CNS-risk presentations (Harrison 22e p.861)
Screening for HIV and hepatitis B and C at diagnosis (risk factors and risk of HBV reactivation with therapy) (Harrison 22e p.861)
redFlags: Burkitt's lymphoma is highly aggressive (doubling time <24 h) — treatment must be initiated quickly and the tumor carries a high risk of tumor lysis syndrome; TLS is most often associated with treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.862, 1014)
Rapid growth of lymph nodes with new B symptoms in known indolent (follicular) lymphoma suggests histologic transformation to DLBCL (~3% per year) (Harrison 22e p.864)

Disease involving paranasal sinuses, testes, breast, kidneys, adrenal glands, or epidural space — and highly aggressive histologies like Burkitt's — carries increased risk of CNS dissemination (Harrison 22e p.861)
Concerning neurologic signs/symptoms warrant lumbar puncture for CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.860)
'Double-hit' high-grade B-cell lymphoma (concurrent MYC and BCL2 rearrangements) has an extremely poor prognosis (median OS ~12-18 months) (Harrison 22e p.862-863)
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable and driven more by histology and clinical parameters than by anatomic stage. Overall 5-year survival for NHL is ~74%. The International Prognostic Index (IPI; age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site) is the best predictor for aggressive NHL: 5-year overall survival ~73%, 51%, 43%, and 26% for 0-1, 2, 3, and 4-5 risk factors. With R-CHOP, ~65-70% of DLBCL patients are cured. The FLIPI predicts follicular lymphoma outcome; most FL patients live 15-20 years but the disease is generally not curable (except localized early-stage), and Burkitt's lymphoma is curable in ~80-90% when treated promptly and correctly (Harrison 22e p.857, 861-862).
pitfalls: Diagnosis requires an adequate tissue sample interpreted by an expert hematopathologist; an inadequate or unrepresentative specimen risks misclassification (e.g., missing coexisting DLBCL within follicular lymphoma or confusing lymphoma with reactive follicular hyperplasia) (Harrison 22e p.860, 863).

The Ann Arbor anatomic staging system is less useful in NHL than in Hodgkin's lymphoma because NHL disseminates widely rather than in an ordered stepwise fashion; histology and the IPI matter more than stage (Harrison 22e p.861).
Treating asymptomatic indolent (follicular) lymphoma does not improve survival — appropriate patients should be observed rather than treated immediately (Harrison 22e p.864).
Failing to anticipate and prevent tumor lysis syndrome before treating rapidly proliferating Burkitt's lymphoma can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.862).

A residual mass on CT after therapy may represent treated fibrosis rather than active disease; PET can help distinguish, but end-of-treatment PET should be delayed (preferably 6-8 weeks after chemotherapy) to avoid false positives (Harrison 22e p.861).
harrison.severityClassification: WHO (WHO-HAEM5) classification of lymphoid malignancies categorizes NHL by cell of origin (mature B-cell vs mature T/NK-cell neoplasms) and entity. Anatomic extent is described by the Ann Arbor staging system (Stage I-IV, with suffix A/B for absence/presence of B symptoms). Prognostic stratification uses the International Prognostic Index (IPI) for aggressive NHL and the FLIPI for follicular lymphoma; follicular lymphoma is also graded I-III by centroblasts per high-power field (Harrison 22e p.857-862).
management: Tailor treatment to histological subtype and pace: observe asymptomatic indolent follicular lymphoma and reserve therapy for symptomatic or high-burden disease
Treat diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with anti-CD20 immunochemotherapy — rituximab combined with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and a corticosteroid — with curative intent
Manage highly aggressive Burkitt lymphoma with intensive multi-agent chemotherapy and central nervous system prophylaxis
Give tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis with hydration and urate-lowering therapy such as allopurinol or rasburicase, plus antimicrobial and growth-factor support during myelosuppression
Use involved-site radiotherapy for localised disease and as consolidation where indicated
Assess response and surveil for relapse with FDG-PET/CT, and biopsy suspected transformation of previously indolent disease
Offer autologous stem-cell transplantation, CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy or bispecific antibodies for relapsed or refractory aggressive lymphoma
Manage through a haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team and escalate urgently for oncological emergencies such as spinal cord compression or superior vena cava obstruction
